t: Largest Prime from Consecutive Prime Sum
o: Starting from 2, sum consecutive primes 2, 2+3, 2+3+5, ... and find the largest such partial sum that is prime and ≤ n. For n = 20 the sums are 2, 5, 10, 17, 28..., and the prime ones ≤ 20 are 2, 5, 17, so the answer is 17. For n = 2 the only sum is 2. Since n ≤ 5·10^5, a sieve plus a running sum with primality lookup is immediate.
k: Sieve once up to n for O(1) primality checks.
Partial sums grow quickly (the sum of primes up to 5e5 exceeds 1e10), so few iterations occur.

a.i: Generate primes in order, accumulate their sum, and after each addition check whether the running sum is ≤ n and prime; track the maximum such value. The running sum is strictly increasing, so the last valid prime sum is the answer.
s: Iterate primes p in increasing order, maintaining s += p.
Stop when s > n; otherwise if is_prime[s], set ans = s.
a.t: O(n log log n) — the sieve dominates; the summation loop runs until the prefix exceeds n

w: Note the running sum must be checked against n before indexing the sieve to avoid out-of-bounds. Pitfall: forgetting that the sum itself must be prime (10 = 2+3+5 is not), and using 32-bit accumulation if extending n. Follow-up: consecutive prime sums starting anywhere (sliding window over primes), or the count of such primes ≤ n.
